title: Resident Evil Reboot Has No Post-Credits Scene, Director Confirms
summary:
If you're the type who sits through ten minutes of credits hoping for a secret scene, you can save yourself the wait with Zach Cregger's new Resident Evil movie. There is no post-credits scene of any kind. Whatever Cregger had to say, he says before the credits roll. The movie is the movie, and that is that.

That's a notable choice in an era when post-credits scenes have become expected franchise fare. After all, Capcom's Resident Evil video games have nine main installments, so there's no shortage of stories to tease. And the first reactions to Cregger's film have been overwhelmingly positive, making a credits scene seem like a no-brainer. But Cregger opted out.

Cregger has quickly become one of horror's biggest names. His genuinely shocking and fun descent into horror, Barbarian, put him on the map, and last year's Oscar-winning smash hit Weapons took him to another level. Now he's putting his stamp on a classic, beloved franchise with a big-screen reboot.

The 2002 Resident Evil movie beat the video game movie curse by delivering a big hit, ultimately birthing a $1 billion franchise with a bunch of sequels. But those movies weren't terribly faithful to the games, and they were never critical darlings. Cregger is attempting to right the ship by taking things in a very different direction. His movie is set in the universe of the games but doesn't adapt any of them directly. Instead, it focuses on new characters and tells a new story. This has been a bit controversial among some hardcore fans, yet early reactions suggest it's worked out rather well.

The synopsis reads: In an all-new story, Resident Evil follows Bryan (Austin Abrams), a medical courier who unwittingly finds himself in an action-packed, non-stop race for survival as one fateful, horrifying night collapses around him in chaos. Cregger co-wrote the screenplay with Shay Hatten (Army of the Dead). Zach Cherry (Severance), Kali Reis (True Detective: Night Country), and Paul Walter Hauser (The Fantastic Four: First Steps) also star.

So feel free to make a break for the lobby as soon as the credits begin without fear of missing out.
why_it_matters: Post-credits scenes are a small detail that reveals something big about modern filmmaking: movies are increasingly built as pieces of long-term franchises rather than standalone stories, so a director refusing to plant a sequel hook is a statement about storytelling versus marketing — and about who really controls a beloved franchise, the studio, the fans, or the filmmaker.

background_read: Post-credits scenes are an old Hollywood trick that Marvel Studios turned into a signature move: Iron Man (2008) ended with Samuel L. Jackson appearing as Nick Fury to hint at a future team-up, and audiences have been sitting through credits ever since. Even earlier, Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986) ended with a famous gag after the credits.

Capcom, the Japanese game company behind Resident Evil, Street Fighter and Monster Hunter, released the first Resident Evil game in 1996; the series is one of the defining examples of 'survival horror', a genre built around scarce resources and creeping dread.

The first Resident Evil movie arrived in 2002, directed by Paul W. S. Anderson and starring Milla Jovovich. It became a surprise hit and grew into a six-film series worth roughly a billion dollars — though fans and critics often complained the films drifted far from the games.

The so-called 'video game movie curse' — the idea that game adaptations are doomed to be bad — was built on flops like Super Mario Bros. (1993), but recent successes such as Sonic the Hedgehog (2020) and The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023) have weakened that rule.

It's worth remembering that post-credits scenes are also marketing: they keep audiences seated, generate social media chatter, and let studios test interest in sequels before greenlighting them. Refusing one is therefore an artistic choice with commercial consequences.

perspectives.description: A self-contained horror film respects the audience's time and makes the story stand on its own rather than serving as an advertisement. Cregger's choice fits his reputation for bold, surprising horror, and the glowing early reactions suggest fans are rewarding that confidence.

perspectives.perspective: Negative — hardcore game fans and franchise strategists
perspectives.description: Some longtime players are frustrated that the reboot keeps the games' universe but adapts none of them, replacing familiar characters with new ones. Others warn that skipping a credits tease removes a cheap but effective way to build buzz and set up potential sequels.

Post-credits scenes are a relatively recent habit, popularised by Marvel's connected-universe model and copied across the industry; for most of cinema history, films simply ended. A horror reboot with a new cast and story also doesn't need a hook, because horror franchises traditionally continue via new settings rather than continuous plot.

If this reboot succeeds, sequels are likely regardless of whether a scene teased them, and Cregger's approach — games' world, original story — could become a template for other adaptations tired of the 'video game movie curse'. The open question is whether hardcore fans will ultimately accept new characters over the ones they grew up with.
